summary: Describes a one-time password authentication system, where each password is used only once so an eavesdropper cannot reuse it. It was replaced by RFC 2289.

eli5.summary: Imagine a list of secret words where each is crossed off after use. Even if a spy sees one, it will not work again.

questions: what is a one-time password system
how do otp systems prevent replay
how do otp systems prevent replay attacks
subtitle: Use a different password for each login, defeating eavesdroppers who capture network traffic.

tldr.problem: When a user sends a login password across the network, an eavesdropper can capture it and use it later to gain access. One-time passwords prevent this replay attack by making each password single-use.
tldr.mechanism: The generator combines a user's secret pass-phrase with a public seed from the server, hashes it many times using a secure hash function, and counts down the number of iterations each time. The server verifies by hashing once and comparing with the stored previous password.
tldr.outcome: Eavesdroppers cannot reuse captured passwords, and the user's pass-phrase never crosses the network. It was replaced by RFC 2289, which clarified the system. The approach is still used in authenticator apps and hardware tokens today.

today: RFC 1938 was superseded by RFC 2289 in 1998, which clarified and refined the specification. The one-time password concept remains in use today in authenticator applications and hardware security tokens, though modern systems often use time-based codes (TOTP) instead of hash-chain-based ones.

sections.title: Authentication Without Revealing Secrets
sections.content:
The RFC describes a one-time password (OTP) system that solves a fundamental problem in network authentication: how to prove you are who you claim to be without sending a reusable secret across the network where eavesdroppers can capture it. The system generates a unique password for each login using a user's secret pass-phrase and information the server sends in the clear.

The key insight is that if a user can generate the next password but an eavesdropper cannot, then replay attacks fail. The system achieves this using a one-way hash function—something easy to compute forward but computationally impossible to reverse.
sections.eli5: You have a secret phrase only you know. Each time you log in, you compute a unique code from that phrase and a number the server tells you. Even if someone hears the code, they cannot work backward to find your secret.

sections.title: How One-Time Passwords Are Generated
sections.content:
The generator starts by concatenating the user's secret pass-phrase with a seed (a public string, typically 1 to 16 characters) provided by the server. This concatenation is passed through a secure hash function like MD5 or SHA-1, and the output is reduced to 64 bits.

A sequence is created by hashing this 64-bit value multiple times. The first password to use is produced by hashing it N times, where N is a counter chosen by the user (often starting at 100 or higher). The next password is produced by hashing N-1 times. After each successful login, the counter decrements by one. An eavesdropper who captures a password has no way to compute the next one because they would need to invert the hash function, which is cryptographically hard.
sections.eli5: Start with your secret phrase plus a public number. Hash it many times to get the first password. For the next login, hash it one fewer time. Each password is different and you cannot work backward.

sections.title: Server Verification and Pass-phrase Changes
sections.content:
The server stores the last password accepted during initialization or the last successful login. To verify a user, it receives the one-time password, decodes it from either six words or hexadecimal format, hashes it once, and compares the result with the stored previous password. If they match, authentication succeeds and the received password becomes the new stored password.

When the counter reaches zero, the user must reinitialize with a new seed or pass-phrase. The RFC requires implementations to support both six-word output (64 bits encoded as six words from a 2048-word dictionary, with a checksum) and hexadecimal (16 hex digits). Generators must support pass-phrases of 10 to 63 characters, and servers must support both formats for interoperability.
sections.eli5: The server keeps the password you used last time. You send the new password. It hashes your password and checks if it matches what it remembered. If yes, it remembers your new password for next time.

sections.title: Scope and Security Limitations
sections.content:
The OTP system protects only against passive eavesdropping and replay attacks on the authentication exchange. It does not provide privacy for the rest of the session, nor does it defend against active attacks like TCP hijacking or social engineering. The security depends entirely on the strength of the underlying hash functions (MD4, MD5, or SHA). To date, none of these have been broken, though MD4 is considered weaker than MD5.

If a server supports multiple hash algorithms, it is only as secure as the weakest one. The system is also vulnerable to race attacks if not defended against: an attacker could listen to most of a one-time password, guess the final word, and try to authenticate before the real user. Servers must prevent simultaneous authentication sessions for the same user.
sections.eli5: This protects you from someone replaying your password, but not from someone hijacking your connection after you log in. Keep your pass-phrase secret and choose a long one.

sections.title: Forms and Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC defines three formats for outputting the one-time password: a six-word format using words from a standard dictionary (easy to type), hexadecimal (easy for software to handle), and an alternative dictionary technique for language-specific implementations. Servers must accept six-word and hexadecimal; they should accept alternative dictionaries. Generators can insert the password into the input stream, make it available for cut-and-paste, or require manual entry.

The OTP system evolved from Bellcore's S/KEY system and was implemented in various tools and hardware tokens for secure remote login over untrusted networks.
sections.eli5: You get the password as six words you can type, hex digits, or cut-and-paste from a program. Different tools can show it different ways as long as they follow the standard.
